common_name: Eva English Ivy (Small Variegated Bird's-Foot Ivy)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or set out container plants in spring, giving the vine a little more light than deep shade so the variegation holds its color.

directions: Eva is one of the smallest-growing English ivy selections, with grey-green, bird's-foot-shaped leaves broadly margined in creamy white. It stays compact and self-branching, making it as useful in a hanging basket or topiary frame as it is trailing along a shaded bed edge. Unlike many variegated ivies it needs a bit more light than full shade to keep its cream edging crisp rather than fading to green. As with other English ivy selections, shear back periodically to remove woody growth and check local rules before planting outdoors, since the species can escape cultivation in mild climates.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or small transplants in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained soil; this compact selection is very cold-hardy and establishes readily.

directions: Duckfoot carries small, matte, rounded leaves with three stubby lobes that resemble webbed duck feet, giving a finer, less aggressive-looking texture than broad-leaved English ivy. Its naturally self-branching habit and modest size make it well suited to groundcover under shrubs, small-space topiary, or softening the edge of a shaded path. It is among the hardier ivy selections, tolerating hard winters better than many cultivars. Shear back every few years to remove old woody stems and keep new growth dense, and monitor for escape into adjacent woodland since the species can naturalize aggressively.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted runners in spring in dry to average shade soil; give this vigorous trailer plenty of room or a barrier, since it spreads by stolons and roots wherever stems touch ground.

directions: Unlike the clumping 'Herman's Pride' selection, Florentinum keeps the wild species' running habit, sending out long trailing stems that root as they travel and form a dense silver-frosted mat over time. Dark green, nettle-like leaves are heavily brushed with silver between the veins, and whorls of soft yellow, snapdragon-like flowers appear in late spring. It tolerates dry shade and competition from tree roots better than most flowering groundcovers, making it a workhorse for difficult woodland edges, but its running vigor means it is best confined to areas where it can roam without crowding out neighboring perennials. Cut back hard in early spring if growth becomes thin or woody at the base.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring or fall in well-drained soil, siting it where its vigorous trailing stems can be contained by an edge or path.

directions: Maculata bears glossy, ovate leaves marked with an irregular yellow-green blotch toward the center, giving a brighter, more variegated look than plain greater periwinkle while keeping the same arching, trailing habit. Violet-blue, pinwheel-shaped flowers appear over a long season from mid-spring into autumn. It roots wherever trailing stems touch soil, making it effective for covering a shaded bank or difficult dry-shade spot, but it spreads with the same vigor as the species and can naturalize aggressively in mild climates if left unchecked. Cut back hard in late winter to renew the planting and keep the variegated color from being hidden under old growth.
